paragraphs.source: \Cref{sec:implementation,sec:properties} give the implementation and proofs. The remaining sections document the benchmark evaluations, ablations, and simulator rollouts.
paragraphs.last_line: tions, ablations, and simulator rollouts.

paragraphs.source: Model training and method evaluation use a server with eight RTX 5090 GPUs. The cost study in \cref{sec:cost} evaluates operation on a single RTX 3090.
paragraphs.last_line: uates operation on a single RTX 3090.

paragraphs.source: The ResNet world models are pretrained offline on action--observation sequences; the \emph{Frozen} setting holds all pretrained weights fixed during test-time execution. For PushObj and PushT, the encoder uses a SmallResNetGeM visual backbone outputting a $d_v=384$-dimensional embedding, paired with a 6-layer action-conditioned Transformer predictor (16 attention heads, feed-forward width 2048, dropout 0.1). Proprioceptive states and 5-step action blocks are mapped through learned 10-dimensional linear embeddings ($d_p=10$). Each training window comprises four observations spaced five control steps apart, where three context frames predict the corresponding one-step-shifted targets. Action embeddings condition the Transformer predictor but are excluded from the reconstruction target.
paragraphs.last_line: dictor but are excluded from the reconstruction target.

paragraphs.source: Let $z_i^o=[z_i^v;z_i^p]\in\R^{d_o}$ denote the concatenated observation latent of total dimension $d_o=d_v+d_p$, let $\hat z_{i+1}^o$ denote the teacher-forced one-step prediction, and let $\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)$ denote the stop-gradient operator. The offline training loss combines mean-squared latent prediction with the Temporal Straightening (TS) training objective~\cite{wang2026straightening}:
paragraphs.last_line: Straightening (TS) training objective [41]:

paragraphs.source: where $\Delta z_i^v=z_{i+1}^v-z_i^v$ and $\lambda_{\rm TS}$ weights the straightening regularizer. The set $\mathcal V$ comprises valid adjacent displacement pairs across the training batch whose Euclidean norms both exceed $10^{-6}$ (using the same numerical floor in the cosine denominator, and setting $\mathcal L_{\rm TS}=0$ if $\mathcal V=\emptyset$). Note that $\mathcal L_{\rm TS}$ acts on observed visual embeddings, whereas the prediction loss averages uniformly across all $d_o$ coordinates (in contrast to the branch-normalized planning metric in \cref{eq:metric}). Target representations are detached via stop-gradient rather than an exponential moving average (EMA).
paragraphs.last_line: gradient rather than an exponential moving average (EMA).

paragraphs.source: For our augmented-data PushObj checkpoints, we train for 3 epochs with $\lambda_{\rm TS}=0.01$, effective batch size 64, and bf16 mixed precision over 1,630,266 training windows and 403,951 validation windows. The visual encoder is optimized using Adam ($\text{lr}=10^{-5}$), while the predictor and action/proprioceptive embedders use AdamW ($\text{lr}=5\times10^{-4}$, weight decay $0.01$), both with $(\beta_1,\beta_2)=(0.9,0.999)$ and constant learning rates. The headline checkpoint additionally trains a detached pixel decoder in the last epoch. Planning uses the same encoder and predictor.
paragraphs.last_line: ning uses the same encoder and predictor.

paragraphs.source: For Maze, we directly evaluate the published SmallResNet checkpoint (without GeM pooling, trained with $\lambda_{\rm TS}=0.001$ and identical Transformer dimensions) without any new offline training. Both released checkpoints correspond to epoch~3 snapshots from a configured 5-epoch schedule.
paragraphs.last_line: to epoch 3 snapshots from a configured 5-epoch schedule.

paragraphs.source: We collect training and validation trajectories for each seen shape using the contact bias and Gaussian noise in \cref{tab:parameters}. Source placements use up to four retries, position jitter of 20 pixels, and orientation jitter of 0.3 radians. The simulator receives pixel displacements divided by 100. We retain valid trajectories with physical contact and displacements under 80 pixels per action block. Training and validation use disjoint source pools. Overlap between released pretraining data and evaluated targets is undocumented.
paragraphs.last_line: training data and evaluated targets is undocumented.

paragraphs.source: MPC optimizes a 25-control horizon and executes the first five controls. Adam runs 100 iterations per replan with a cosine schedule from 0.1 to zero. Planning starts from zero displacements, then warm-starts by shifting the unexecuted suffix and padding with zeros. No action noise is added.
paragraphs.last_line: suffix and padding with zeros. No action noise is added.

paragraphs.source: AdaJEPA updates after each executed block using the five most recent transition segments and one-step prediction loss without straightening. It updates the last Transformer block, final normalization layer, and encoder output projection. Learning rates are $5\times10^{-4}$ for the predictor and $10^{-5}$ for the encoder. Each update starts a fresh Adam optimizer and enables dropout only during adaptation. Each episode starts from the offline checkpoint.
paragraphs.last_line: starts from the offline checkpoint.

paragraphs.source: PushObj and PushT require both the joint pusher--object position error and the wrapped orientation error to fall below the tolerances in \cref{tab:parameters} at a replan boundary. Maze uses the goal-distance tolerance. Runs stop on success, with per-control stopping for the medium-route protocol in \cref{tab:maze-medium-threshold}.
paragraphs.last_line: control stopping for the medium-route protocol in Tab. 20.

paragraphs.source: The controller measures prediction loss, updates AdaJEPA when enabled, then detects stalls with the updated encoder. A detected stall stores the current observation. With first-stall activation, the memory and task-specific correction take effect at the next plan. The loss gate in \cref{eq:gate} releases stored memories once the loss plateaus at a stall. Subsequent stalls renew the temporary reweighting, and stored memories last for the episode. Warm-up lasts ten replans on PushObj and four in the original loss-gated Maze protocol.
paragraphs.last_line: nal loss-gated Maze protocol.

We reuse non-triggered trajectories and rerun all tasks for permanent reweighting. The exact two-sided McNemar test compares discordant successes. Rescue and harm count paired tasks that switch from failure to success and from success to failure, respectively.
paragraphs.last_line: success to failure, respectively.

paragraphs.source: The PushT benchmark evaluates a common, fixed list of 50 start--goal pairs across clean observations and six visual distribution shifts: Gaussian blur ($\sigma=2$), salt-and-pepper impulse noise (1\% salt, 1\% pepper), darkened lighting (intensity scale $0.9$), and RGB recoloring (to red) of the pusher agent, manipulated T-block, or background goal anchor. The ResNet ECP configuration is transferred from PushObj ($\gamma_{\rm hi}=0.15$) without tuning.
paragraphs.last_line: PushObj (γ= 0.15) without tuning.

paragraphs.source: Changing the approach to an object can complete alignment; leaving a revisited corridor can open a route to the goal. Both behaviors use the recent stall to condition the next planning objective.
paragraphs.last_line: next planning objective.

paragraphs.source: \captionof{figure}{\textbf{ECP recovers stalls across seven PushObj shapes and three Maze tasks.} Brown and teal paths trace planning without and with ECP from the same start (circle) to their endpoints (cross or diamond). Stars mark goals and dots mark five-control blocks. Frozen fixes the pretrained ResNet, while AdaJEPA updates it online.}
paragraphs.last_line: fixes the pretrained ResNet, while AdaJEPA updates it online.

paragraphs.source: \Cref{fig:maze-detour} examines this mechanism at a wall. In the adaptive-model example, ECP leaves a revisited corridor, temporarily increases goal distance, and rounds the wall before reaching the target. The frozen-model pair shows recovery without weight updates. The distance traces link these detours to subsequent progress. Control indices expose motion inside a planning block; five controls equal one step. Both plots use actual executed trajectories.
paragraphs.last_line: step. Both plots use actual executed trajectories.

paragraphs.source: ECP uses the current representation to identify revisited states. Shift-invariant features could extend correction to stronger appearance changes. Source-disjoint tasks and held-out training seeds provide a next test of transfer~\cite{henderson2018matters,agarwal2021statistical}. Recovery trajectories also offer supervision for chunked policies~\cite{zhao2023act}, reusing corrections across episodes.
paragraphs.last_line: policies [46], reusing corrections across episodes.

paragraphs.source: The PushT pairs in \cref{fig:pusht-rollouts} hold the LeWM weights, task, and execution budget fixed while switching ECP on or off. The red-agent case changes the pusher's appearance; the red-goal case changes the target cue. These examples test whether execution feedback can recover a stalled plan when either the pusher or the goal cue changes in appearance.
paragraphs.last_line: goal cue changes in appearance.

paragraphs.source: ECP completes both tasks while native planning repeats local motion until the control limit. The snapshots show the intervening physical interaction and final alignment, complementing the aggregate visual-shift results. Each sequence ends at its actual stopping point, with the shared start and goal in the left column and four aligned execution frames displayed to its right.
paragraphs.last_line: frames displayed to its right.

paragraphs.source: \captionof{figure}{\textbf{ECP recovers PushT under color shifts.} Paired runs use the same fixed LeWM, start, goal, and 150-control budget. Brown/teal label planning without/with ECP; frame numbers count executed controls. ECP succeeds under both red-agent and red-goal shifts, while native planning exhausts its budget. The left column shows the shared start and goal.}

paragraphs.source: \captionof{figure}{\textbf{Maze recoveries with adaptive and frozen ResNet world models.} Each row shows five recorded frames from one run. Columns align the two planners by executed control. Trails cover the preceding four controls, the white ring marks the agent, and the pale ring marks the goal. In (a), Ours briefly moves farther away to round a wall and reaches the goal at control 90. In (b), Ours reaches the goal at control 43 with the pretrained ResNet held fixed. Both native runs exhaust the 150-control budget.}
